stimulus.text:
The British print shows four Loyalists hanged from a tree branch, with the words “Recommended to Congress by Lord S—” written above them. Below, three Native figures attack Loyalists: one holds a rope and says “I have them all in a String,” one holds a knife and says “I'll scalp him,” and one raises a tomahawk and says “I'll tomahawk the Dog.” A kneeling Loyalist cries, “O Cruel Fate! is this the Return for Our Loyalty.” The title reads “The Savages let loose, OR The Cruel FATE of the LOYALISTS,” with the captions “Is this a Peace, when Loyalists must bleed?” and “It is a Bloody Piece of work indeed.”
— The Savages Let Loose, London, 1783 (sold by W. Humphrey, 227 Strand)

stem: The print's point of view is best described as that of

options.text: American Patriots celebrating a victory over the British
options.misconception: Patriots would not mourn Loyalists; the print weeps for them and asks if this is a peace, which is a British complaint.

options.text: French observers praising the new American republic
options.misconception: No French voice appears; the print is sold in London and speaks for Loyalists, not for France.

options.text: British sympathizers warning that the peace abandons the Loyalists
Native leaders protesting the loss of their lands
options.misconception: Native peoples are shown as attackers, not as speakers; the print uses them as a threat, not as its voice.

rationales.C: The print was sold in London in 1783, and its captions mourn the Loyalists: “Is this a Peace, when Loyalists must bleed?” It warns that the peace leaves them to their enemies.
rationales.A: Celebration would show Patriots triumphant; this print shows Loyalists hanged and begs the reader's pity.
rationales.B: France is absent from the print; its audience is British, and its subject is the Loyalists' fate.
rationales.D: Native peoples are drawn as the danger, not given a voice; the print speaks for Loyalists, not for them.
rationales.general:
1. Read the captions. “Is this a Peace, when Loyalists must bleed?” — a complaint, not a celebration.
2. Find the seller. A London print shop, 1783, the year of the peace.
3. Ask whose fate it mourns. The Loyalists, hanged above and attacked below.
Remember: a print's point of view lives in its captions — read who is pitied and who is blamed.
